rows.title: U.S. population growth is slowing. The immigration crackdown is a major factor
rows.standfirst: Congressional forecasters have lowered their projection for U.S. population growth over the next decade by 7 million people as a result of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown as well as falling birth rates.

rows.title: How Black hair care grew Black power
rows.standfirst: The Afro is one of the most iconic hairstyles of the last century. And one of its main ingredients was a hair product – Afro Sheen. But Afro Sheen did so much more than make Black afros shine. It was the money behind the television show Soul Train, it helped fuel the civil rights movement – all because of an entrepreneur named George Johnson.

rows.title: It's not just oil: How else Wall Street might benefit from Trump's Venezuela actions
rows.standfirst: Oil companies and their shareholders may benefit from President Trump's military action in Venezuela — but it also could benefit many other U.S. investors.

rows.title: The world has too much oil right now. Will companies want Venezuela's?
rows.standfirst: Crude prices are low. Companies are being cautious. But huge reserves — particularly of the heavy, viscous oil Venezuela has in abundance — remain appealing.

rows.title: Can you trust you're getting the same grocery prices as someone else?
rows.standfirst: When you're in a grocery store nowadays, chances are your data is being collected. From a swipe of the loyalty card to the purchase of an ice cream pint, your data tells stores what you like, how much they should stock, and more.

rows.title: Trump Mobile's golden phone remains nowhere to be found
rows.standfirst: A golden phone that President Donald Trump's family business promised to release last year remains mysteriously under wraps as the technology industry serves up a glut of new gadgets at CES in Las Vegas this week.

rows.title: Trump says US to get 30 million to 50 million barrels of oil from Venezuela at market price
rows.standfirst: Trump pledged to use proceeds from the sale of this oil "to benefit the people" of both countries.

rows.title: Attempting to predict the economy in 2026
rows.standfirst: Economists may have a pretty dismal record with predictions. But we're still interested in what they see in their non-existent crystal balls.

rows.title: How cocaine smuggling through Latin America really works
rows.standfirst: Former Venezuelan leader, Nicolás Maduro, appeared in a New York court yesterday. He’s facing drug-trafficking and weapons charges after the U.S. abducted him and his wife in an explosive operation over the weekend. But is there any credibility to the drug-trafficking accusations? And what does the cocaine supply chain look like in 2026?

rows.title: New redesigned coins marking nation's 250th birthday begin circulating today
rows.standfirst: New coins marking the United States' 250th anniversary begin circulating this week. The Trump administration tweaked the design of some coins and is considering a dollar coin featuring the president.

rows.title: Why China pulled the plug on Japan
rows.standfirst: Japan’s new prime minister Sanae Takaichi made waves last fall after saying her country might intervene if China invaded Taiwan. In response, China launched state-organized boycotts against Japan — canceling concerts, restricting seafood imports, and even recalling pandas. Today on the show, what does it look like for a state to organize a boycott, and does it work? Related episodes:

rows.title: Venezuela’s recent economic history (Update)
rows.standfirst: We’ve been checking in on the economic conditions in Venezuela for about a decade now. In response to the U.S. strike and the capture of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro this weekend, we’re re-surfacing this episode with an update.

rows.title: Venezuela’s economic descent (Updated)
rows.standfirst: At The Indicator, we’ve been following the conditions in Venezuela over the years. In 2024 we covered how Venezuela’s economy went into freefall, and have been checking in with an economist there frequently — including after the U.S. attacked over the weekend, deposing its leader Nicolás Maduro.

rows.title: Can the global economy handle a world with fewer kids?
rows.standfirst: Ashley and Nick Evancho say raising their young daughter, Sophia, is one of the most joyous things they've ever done. But the Evanchos also made a decision that's increasingly common for families in the U.S. and around the world: one is enough. The trend is leading to populations that are dramatically older, and beginning to shrink, in many of the world's biggest economies.

rows.title: We resolve to watch these 2026 indicators
rows.standfirst: 2025 is finally over.

rows.title: How have prices changed in a year? NPR checked 114 items at Walmart
rows.standfirst: We found the effects of tariffs and extreme weather, relief (finally!) in the egg cooler, plus one case of shrinkflation.

rows.title: How much money President Trump and his family have made
rows.standfirst: Before President Donald Trump’s first term, he was in a “tight spot” financially, according to New Yorker writer David Kirkpatrick. At the start of his second term, David says, Trump was in an “even tighter” spot. But after just six months into his second term, Trump’s financial situation started looking really good.

rows.title: Can a good story change economic reality?
rows.standfirst: Economic decisions aren’t only driven by hard data. A compelling story can change economic behavior and outcomes. In today’s episode, we explore real-world examples of “narrative economics” like how the Suez Canal ended up getting built. And we ask: why do narratives sometimes matter more than truth or data? Related episodes:

rows.title: China's trade surplus surges 20% to a record $1.2 trillion, even with Trump's tariffs
rows.standfirst: China's trade surplus surged to a record of almost $1.2 trillion in 2025, the government said Wednesday, as exports to other countries made up for slowing shipments to the U.S. under President Donald Trump's onslaught of higher tariffs.

rows.title: FTC accuses AI search engine of 'rampant consumer deception'
rows.standfirst: Federal officials say a company that operates hundreds of landing pages for AI answers is running an operation that has duped thousands of users, who were unable to stop costly monthly charges.

rows.title: One Fed battle after another
rows.standfirst: Over the weekend, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell said the Department of Justice served the Fed with grand jury subpoenas. Powell says it’s all a sham. But the stakes are unprecedented: A potential criminal indictment. Central bank independence. Today on the show, the administration’s case against the Fed. How did we get here? And what comes next?

rows.title: California fire victims say fighting with insurance companies has delayed rebuilding
rows.standfirst: Wildfires last January destroyed communities around Los Angeles. Homeowners say recovery has been slowed by fights with insurers to get their claims paid.

rows.title: What to know about Trump's ugly feud with the Federal Reserve
rows.standfirst: A Justice Department probe of the Federal Reserve marks the latest escalation in the Trump administration's effort to bend the independent central bank to the president's will.

rows.title: Offshore wind developer prevails in U.S. court as Trump calls wind farms 'losers'
rows.standfirst: A federal judge ruled Monday that work on a major offshore wind farm can resume, handing the industry at least a temporary victory as President Trump seeks to shut it down.

rows.title: Trump calls for a 10% cap on credit card interest rates
rows.standfirst: With credit card interest rates near modern highs, President Trump says he wants to cap the rates for one year.

rows.title: How IVF has led to a record number of single moms in their 40s
rows.standfirst: Who gets to be a parent has been reshaped by IVF: Single women in their 40s are increasingly opting to become moms.

rows.title: How far can philanthropy go to fill government gaps?
rows.standfirst: While Americans are known for their generosity, the U.S. government, increasingly, is not. The Trump administration’s cuts to SNAP benefits among other aid programs have forced states, foundations and donors to fill the gaps. But can they? On today’s show, the limits of philanthropic efforts to supplant federal aid.

rows.title: DOJ subpoenas the Federal Reserve in an escalating pressure campaign
rows.standfirst: The Justice Department has subpoenaed the Fed over Chair Jerome Powell's testimony over the central bank's headquarters renovation. Powell calls it part of a pressure campaign over interest rates.

rows.title: 2026 looks ominous for media, from Hollywood to journalism
rows.standfirst: Critic at large Eric Deggans says that in 2026, audiences have more power than they realize to determine the future of news and entertainment.

rows.title: So are we in an AI bubble? Here are clues to look for.
rows.standfirst: Are we in an AI bubble? That’s the $35 trillion dollar question right now as the stock market soars higher and higher. The problem is that bubbles are famously hard to spot. But some economists say they may have found some telltale clues.

rows.title: When designing a GAME, what's in a name?
rows.standfirst: Planet Money has teamed up with the company Exploding Kittens to make a board game inspired by the legendary economics paper The Market for Lemons. We’ve decided we want a mass-appeal party game that quietly sneaks in the economics, so that we can report from inside a world that no other Planet Money project has entered: the real shelves at real big box retail stores.

rows.title: Supreme Court doubtful of Trump claim he can fire Fed governors by fiat
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration wants the authority to fire Lisa Cook, a Federal Reserve governor. Experts say that would undermine the independence of the central bank.

rows.title: Trump administration claims offshore wind poses a threat. But it won't say how.
rows.standfirst: The Interior Department said pausing construction of offshore wind farms would allow the government agencies to work with project developers to mitigate potential risks. But wind companies say the administration isn't sharing information about newly-discovered threats.

rows.title: It's showdown time for the Fed's independence at the Supreme Court
rows.standfirst: At issue are President Trump's efforts to break with 112 years of law and precedent by firing Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve's governing board.

rows.title: 1 year into Trump's new term, an agency that protects your finances is 'hanging by a thread'
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration has ordered work stoppages and layoffs and has tried cutting off funding to effectively dismantle the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

rows.title: Is Greenland really an untapped land of riches?
rows.standfirst: President Donald Trump is dead set on acquiring Greenland, and while national security is the stated reason, the country’s untapped mineral wealth could offer another explanation. Today on the show: is Greenland really an untapped land of riches? We talk to one Australian geologist who discovered the great costs and potential rewards of extracting these minerals himself. Related episodes:

rows.title: Trump promised to cut energy bills in half. One year later, has he delivered?
rows.standfirst: Cheap gasoline, yes. Drill, baby, drill? Not so much. And electricity bills are going up, not down.

rows.title: Are defense firms showering their shareholders with too much money?
rows.standfirst: In early January, President Donald Trump signed an executive order threatening bans on defense contractors paying dividends or buying their stock back.

rows.title: They quit their day jobs to bet on current events. A look inside the prediction market mania
rows.standfirst: Prediction market apps are thriving in Trump's second term, with traders betting on migrant deportations to election outcomes. A community of young, mostly male and very online traders are driving the industry's bonanza.

rows.title: Chevron, Venezuela and the Paradox of Plenty
rows.standfirst: Venezuela and Chevron have perhaps one of the strangest partnerships … ever? Chevron, one of the world’s most famous and profitable oil corporations, has for decades, been plugging away in Venezuela, one of the world’s most famous and infamous socialist countries.

rows.title: It took 75 governors to elect a woman. Abigail Spanberger is now at Virginia's helm
rows.standfirst: Spanberger, a former CIA officer and three-term congresswoman, is breaking long-held traditions on inauguration day. She says she wanted her swearing-in to showcase the state's modern vibrancy.

rows.title: December board game update
rows.standfirst: This is a short update on the Planet Money Board Game project.

rows.title: Canada agrees to cut tariff on Chinese EVs in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products
rows.standfirst: Breaking with the United States, Canada has agreed to cut its 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Friday.

rows.title: ICE influencers, a world-record trade surplus, and the moon goes nuclear
rows.standfirst: Welcome back to Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Verizon just had a big outage. Here's what we know
rows.standfirst: Verizon says a software problem caused the glitch and it is conducting a postmortem, but experts say outages are "a fact of life" these days.

rows.title: With decades-long restrictions lifted, a Pakistani brewery has started exporting beer
rows.standfirst: Drinking is illegal for Pakistan's Muslim majority, but Murree Brewery's beer has long been available to non-Muslims and foreigners there. Now it's being exported to the U.K., Japan and Portugal. Is the U.S. next?

rows.title: Can Trump make buying a home more affordable?
rows.standfirst: Book tour dates and ticket info here .

rows.title: 'Washington Post' journalists plea to Bezos: Don't gut our newsroom
rows.standfirst: Members of the newspaper's union say they have been warned the company could cut as many as 300 jobs, although no announcement has been made.

rows.title: Feds arrest Don Lemon, Minnesota journalist and 2 others over church protest
rows.standfirst: Lemon was arrested by U.S. agents days after covering an anti-ICE protest at a St. Paul, Minn., church. U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi called the protest a "coordinated attack."

rows.title: Trump taps Kevin Warsh to lead the Federal Reserve
rows.standfirst: Trump plans to nominate Kevin Warsh to be the next chair of the Federal Reserve, when Jerome Powell's term expires in May. The president has been pushing the central bank to slash interest rates.

rows.title: Kari Lake promotes Trump on Voice of America. Does that break the law?
rows.standfirst: Critics say U.S. Agency for Global Media's Kari Lake risks making Voice of America sound like a propaganda outlet in her remarks on the air praising President Trump.

rows.title: Trump thinks a weaker dollar is great for America. Is he right?
rows.standfirst: The president said this week that the value of the dollar is "great" despite a sharp tumble since last year. That may be true for certain parts of the economy — but not others.

rows.title: Kalshi in court over 19 federal lawsuits. What's the future of prediction markets?
rows.standfirst: Apps that let people wager on current events have experienced explosive growth in Trump's second term. But one of the leading markets is tied up in lawsuits that cloud the industry's future.

rows.title: A huge EU-India deal, Heated Rivalry, and a hefty $200k to Olympians
rows.standfirst: It’s … Indicators of the Week! Our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: Medicare Advantage insurers face new curbs on overcharges in Trump plan
rows.standfirst: Federal officials have a plan that could curb billions of dollars in overpayments to Medicare Advantage plans. But will they follow through on it?

rows.title: Caregivers for the elderly could lose wage protections under Trump proposal
rows.standfirst: The Labor Department has proposed rescinding an Obama-era rule that gave home care workers the right to overtime pay and other wage protections. The administration says the rule made care too costly.

rows.title: Hawaii’s worker shortage goes NUTS
rows.standfirst: Macadamia nuts. Labor shortages. Volcanoes. All that might sound like econ Mad Libs, but they’re all connected to the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco’s entry into the Beige Book this month: labor shortages are hurting macadamia nut harvests in Hawaii. On today’s show, we take a vacation and talk to someone on the Big Island who runs a macadamia nut farm. He calls them “mac nuts.” Related episodes:

rows.title: Tesla profits slumped 46% last year, as it lost its crown as the top EV seller
rows.standfirst: The company announced it was ending production of its higher-end Model S and Model Y, and turning that production space over to making humanoid robots.

rows.title: This housing program helped kids escape poverty — by changing who they befriended
rows.standfirst: In the 1990s, Congress created HOPE VI, a program that demolished old public housing projects and replaced them with more up-to-date ones. But the program went further than just improving public housing buildings. HOPE VI was designed to transform neighborhoods with concentrated poverty into neighborhoods that attracted people with different incomes. Some people who moved to HOPE VI neighborhoods earned too much to qualify for public housing. And some even paid for market-rate housing. The idea was that this would help create new opportunities for the low-income people who lived there and even lift people out of poverty.

rows.title: Fed holds interest rates steady, taking a pause from rate cuts to assess the economy
rows.standfirst: The central bank cut rates at its three previous meetings in an effort to support the job market. But with inflation still elevated, the Fed is cautious about additional rate cuts.
